newsitem.title: USA: Nike says apparel shipments behind schedule.
newsitem.headline: Nike says apparel shipments behind schedule.

text.p: Nike Inc's U.S. apparel shipments have fallen two to three weeks behind schedule due to high demand and a warehouse fire, Nike President and Chief Operating Officer Tom Clarke said on Monday.
"It is a concern in terms of meeting our retailers' needs," Clarke said in a conference call with analysts and reporters.

Nike Chief Financial Officer Bob Falcone said in the call that without the June fire, which shut the company's Memphis, Tenn., distribution facility for about a week, sales in the quarter just ended would have been about $40 million higher.
He said most of the shortfall would be made up by the end of the current fiscal second quarter, which began September 1.
Clarke also said he expected the company's sales expense ratio in the current fiscal year to be about the same as last year's 24.6 percent.
That would be slightly higher than the fiscal first quarter, when sales, general and administrative expenses were 23.2 percent of sales.
Falcone said the first quarter was the eighth straight quarter of double-digit revenue increases.
"We're very excited about the continued strength of the U.S. brand and our dominance at retail," Falcone said.

Despite the maturity of the U.S. footwear market, Nike athletic footwear sales were up 27 percent in the first quarter over the year-earlier period, and the company has raised shoe prices by seven to eight percent, officials said.

Sales of men's basketball shoes, the company's biggest category, rose 48 percent to over $200 million in the quarter. Men's running shoes were up 67 percent and women's sports shoes were up 58 percent.
Nike also saw strong double-digit increases in most overseas markets in the quarter, particularly when the figures were adjusted for fluctuations in the dollar, Falcone said.
On a constant-dollar basis, European footwear sales were up about 30 percent, Asia-Pacific sales were up 62 percent, and sales in the Americas, excluding the United States, were up 23 percent.
Clarke said that in countries that use the company's future-order system, more than 90 percent of sales are accounted for by the advance orders.
He indicated that the company would prefer that the ratio fall closer to 85 percent, but capacity constraints limit the amount of "at-once" orders the company is able to ship.
